d.title: The DPO family, organised by what each one deletes
d.caption: Reading the family as a sequence of **deletions** makes it memorable. DPO removed the reward model and the RL loop; ORPO additionally removes the **reference model and the separate SFT stage**, so a base model goes straight to aligned in one pass; KTO removes the need for **pairs**, which is the only one that matters if your data is thumbs-up/thumbs-down; SimPO removes the reference model and length-normalises; IPO removes Bradley-Terry's assumption that preferences are transitive and deterministic.

d.title: ORPO learns the good answer and pushes away from the bad one in one step
d.caption: Two terms: ordinary SFT loss on the chosen response, plus λ times an **odds-ratio** penalty on the rejected one. The first is why there is no separate SFT stage — the SFT is happening here — and the second is why there is no reference model, because an odds ratio is computed within the policy rather than against a frozen copy. Which makes it the cheapest member of the family in memory and the one with the fewest moving parts.

nodes.label: Term 2: odds-ratio penalty on the rejected

d.title: KTO borrows its loss from prospect theory, deliberately
d.caption: The value function is over **gains and losses relative to a reference point, with losses weighted more heavily than equivalent gains** — and that asymmetry is a deliberate model of human judgement rather than a mathematical convenience. What it buys practically is that the data can be **individual labels**: a thumbs-down needs no matching thumbs-up on the same prompt, which is what production feedback actually looks like.

nodes.label: Losses weigh more than gains
nodes.sub: a model of judgement, not convenience

d.title: SimPO fixes length bias at the loss rather than in the data
d.caption: 7.6 measured where DPO's length bias comes from: the implicit reward is a **sum over response tokens**, so for a per-token gain of d nats it equals β·d·n — **a long mediocre response collects the same reward as a short excellent one.** SimPO divides by length, turning the sum into an average, and adds a target margin γ. Which is the right place to fix it: filtering long responses out of the data treats the symptom, and normalising removes the incentive.

nodes.label: DPO's implicit reward is a sum
The incentive is gone, not filtered
nodes.sub: which is the right place to fix it

d.title: The siblings are the baseline
d.caption: PPO needs a value network because the reward arrives once, on the final token, so something must estimate how good each completion was **expected** to be — and that estimator is a second trainable LLM costing **104.3 GB at 7B**. GRPO's move is to generate G completions for the same prompt and use **the group's own mean and standard deviation** as the baseline. The siblings answer the question the critic was trained to answer, for free, and with no regression to fit.

nodes.label: The reward arrives on the last token
PPO: train a critic to estimate it

d.title: A discrepancy worth tracking down: n or n-1
d.caption: Six binary rewards, three correct. Standardising them gives advantages of **±0.9129 with torch's default (unbiased, n−1)** and **±1.0 with the population standard deviation**, which is what a hand calculation produces. The ratio is exactly √(5/6) = 0.9129. Neither is wrong — but the two differ by 8.7% on every advantage in the batch, which is a systematic scaling of the gradient, and it is the kind of difference that gets attributed to a hyperparameter.

d.title: Deleting the critic is 44% of the memory
d.caption: PPO holds four models at 7B — policy and critic trained, reference and reward model frozen — for **234.7 GB**. Dropping the critic takes it to 130.4 GB, and dropping the reward model too, which RLVR does, reaches **117.3 GB: the same as DPO**. So GRPO with a verifier costs exactly what the offline method costs while keeping the online exploration that 7.6 identified as PPO's one irreplaceable property.

steps.code: GRPO + RLVR - no RM at all

d.title: The thing GRPO deletes is hardest to do well exactly where it deletes it
d.caption: This is the cleanest answer to *why GRPO for reasoning*, and it is not just that it is cheaper. A critic predicts expected future reward from a **partial** sequence; with a continuous reward model that regression is tractable, and **with a binary verifier it is not** — predicting a 0/1 outcome from half a proof is close to hopeless. Meanwhile the group mean gets *easier* in that regime: the mean of six binary outcomes is an unbiased estimate of the pass rate, which is exactly the baseline you want.

d.title: A verifier has no region where the gradient vanishes
d.caption: 7.4 measured why a learned reward model is exploitable: the Bradley-Terry gradient is 1−σ(g), so it **vanishes once a gap is large and nothing constrains how big a correct gap becomes**. A verifier has no such region. `extract_boxed(completion) == gold` is either true or not, and **no amount of length, confidence, flattery or formatting changes the answer** — so you can optimise against it much harder, and the KL leash becomes a mild regulariser against degeneration rather than the load-bearing defence it is in RLHF.

nodes.label: A verifier is true or false
So optimise much harder

nodes.label: And the KL leash becomes mild

d.title: Binary rewards make the zero-advantage case the common one
d.caption: 7.8's degenerate case is that GRPO produces **exactly zero advantage when all G samples get the same reward** — the group standard deviation is zero and there is nothing to standardise against. With a learned reward model, continuous scores make exact ties rare. **With a 0/1 verifier they are the common case**: an easy problem gives six passes, a hard one gives six failures, and both batches contribute no gradient at all. So the curriculum has to be chosen to keep problems near the pass-rate middle.

d.title: Four stages, and why stage 3 is not circular
d.caption: Re-training on the model's own correct outputs sounds circular and is not, because **RL and SFT move weights differently**: RL gives a noisy, high-variance signal, and SFT gives dense imitation. So stage 3 **consolidates** — it takes the behaviour RL discovered stochastically and makes it the default, which is cheaper and more stable than continuing to run RL. It is the same mechanism as 7.13's finding that distilling a reasoning model's traces beats training the smaller model with RL directly.

d.title: Nobody told it to think longer
d.caption: Given only *correct answer = 1* as a signal, **response length grew on its own** over training. No part of the reward mentions length, reasoning steps, backtracking or verification — and behaviours like *"Wait, let me reconsider…"* appeared **without ever being demonstrated**. The mechanism is unglamorous and worth stating: longer reasoning raises the pass rate, the pass rate is the only thing rewarded, so length rises as a side effect of the thing that was optimised.

nodes.label: So length grows on its own
A side effect of what was optimised

d.title: Five ways to spend compute at inference instead of in training
d.caption: 7.2 was entirely about the first factor and its awkward arithmetic — over-training an 8B past Chinchilla cost more than training a 70B optimally. **The second factor needs no retraining at all**, which makes it the cheapest quality lever available to someone who did not train the model. The cost multipliers are the thing to read: longer chain-of-thought is 2–20× output tokens, and self-refine at k rounds is 2k×.
cells: expand and prune with a PRM

d.title: The self-consistency claim turns on something nobody states
d.caption: "A 60%-accurate model voting over 8 samples reaches about 78%" is simulatable, and the thing it depends on is **whether the wrong answers agree**. If every error is the same wrong answer, voting reaches only **71.9%** — below the claim — because the majority is reliably wrong. If errors are diverse the same vote reaches **98.6%**. The published figure sits between the two, so it is quietly an assumption about error structure rather than about accuracy.

d.title: Accuracy per unit cost falls monotonically, and the big model is last
d.caption: The sampling ladder buys real accuracy — 60.0% to **99.3% at 16 samples** — and the right-hand column is the one that decides anything: accuracy per unit cost falls at every step, from 0.6000 to 0.0621. And the big model is **worse still at 0.0425**, which is the actual argument for test-time compute: not that it is efficient, but that it is **less inefficient than a 20× model** while needing no retraining and no new deployment.

d.title: Route it to the hard tail, do not enable it everywhere
d.caption: Test-time compute is the cheapest quality lever because it needs no retraining, and **it trades latency for accuracy** — so it belongs on the hard tail of traffic rather than on every request. Enabling it globally pays the 8× on the majority of queries that were already correct at one sample, which is where the per-unit-cost column of §03 becomes a bill. The routing decision is 3.10's, applied to a different axis.

nodes.label: Pay 8x on the hard tail only
